fields_add.community: Downstream of the Phase 1 dams, a separate compensation stream covered villages that lost river resources to the reduced flows. The World Bank's Phase 1B completion report says 54 communities in the river reaches nearest the dams received a first payment under the In-Stream Flow Requirement policy, that communities in the reaches further down were still being organised, and that others were to be assessed later through monitoring. One of the same report's results tables says instead that 23 of the 54 local legal entities established in those reaches received the payment, in 2004. Among the claimants is the U Khopo Maliba-Matšo Society in Bobete, in Thaba-Tseka district, registered in 2003 and with over six hundred members, by the Court of Appeal's account. The losses the policy compensates, as the Society's founding affidavit lists them, are riverine resources, firewood and construction timber, fish resources, wild vegetables, medicinal plant resources and animal forage.
fields_add.outcome: The Bank's Phase 1B loan was IBRD-43390, US$45 million, approved 4 June 1998, effective 9 June 1999 and closed 31 December 2006, of which US$21.66 million was disbursed. The complainants' Inspection Panel request of 23 April 1998 describes a $50 million loan for Phase 1B as then before the Executive Directors; the Bank's completion report gives the loan as approved at US$45 million. The Phase 1 In-Stream Flow Requirement policy was developed during that project. The Bank's completion report says the flow studies were undertaken during implementation of Phase 1B, after the environmental impact assessment and the engineering designs had been completed. Its results tables give the study as completed in August 2000 in one place and October 2000 in another, and the Authority's own summary printed in the same report says the studies started in 1996 and were completed in 2001. That summary says the policy and its procedures were approved in June 2003, while the Bank's results tables say they were adopted in July 2003. The report says the project paid M27 million as a first ten-year payment under the policy for predicted downstream losses of natural resources in the proximal reaches. Compliance with the policy was a safeguards matter for the Bank: the report says safeguard performance was rated satisfactory in only four of the 13 supervision reports where it was rated, mainly because of non-compliance with the policy, delays in formulating the approach to stage 3 resettlement and weak performance of other social protection programmes. On compensation as a whole, and excluding income restoration and training programmes, the report says M83 million had been paid out for project-related losses, with payments to continue, where still owed, for a further 40 years. Clause 7.7 of the policy, as quoted by the Court of Appeal, provides for two payments: the first for the period from the policy taking effect to 2013, and a second and final payment of the balance owing, calculated as a present value over 50 years and taking into consideration the findings of the ten-year review. The clause as quoted does not itself name 2013 as a payment date. That the second payment fell due in 2013 is how the parties and the courts read it: the Society's founding affidavit says the second payment should have been made in 2013, its counsel called 2013 the due date, and the Court of Appeal said payment of the second tranche was due in 2013. The second payment did not come. The Authority ran a monitoring programme from 2003 to 2013 and engaged consultants in 2013. Its answer gives the consultants' report as dated 24 June 2014 and its counsel's heads of argument give it as 4 June 2014. The report concluded there was no justification for a further payment, the Authority's Environmental Panel of Experts confirmed that, and the Authority decided not to pay. The Authority's answer says the first payment had been made against presumed losses, because baseline data was inadequate to predict ecosystem service losses such as woody vegetation and fish from the reduced flows; its counsel put the same point in the heads of argument. The Society sued in the High Court, where Makara J ordered the Authority to make the second and final payment; GroundUp dates that order 19 March 2025. The Court of Appeal of Lesotho dismissed the Authority's appeal in C of A (CIV) 28/2025, carried by the Lesotho Legal Information Institute as [2025] LSCA 57, heard 13 October 2025 and delivered 7 November 2025, before Mosito P, Sakoane CJ and Musonda AJA. The court held that the duty to compensate arises by operation of law, from section 17(1)(c) of the Constitution, Article 7(18) of the project Treaty and sections 44 to 46 of the Lesotho Highlands Development Authority Order 1986, and so cannot be negated or deferred by administrative policy. It held that the decision to discontinue compensation without meaningful consultation of the Bobete community was procedurally unfair and substantively unlawful. In his concurring judgment, at paragraph 49, Mosito P wrote: “Compensation delayed for over a decade is, in practical terms, compensation denied.” The judgment's flynote puts the same point as “compensation delayed for over a decade amounts to compensation denied”. The order dismissed the appeal with costs, confirmed the High Court's order and directed the Authority to commence payment within ninety days. It states no sum; one of the questions Mosito P set out was whether an order to pay the “second and final tranche” is competent where no sum is quantified. GroundUp reported on 10 February 2026 that the ninety days expired on 7 February 2026 with no payment made, that the Society had received about M2.7 million for the first period and other associations between M500,000 and M3 million, and that the Authority's spokesperson Mpho Brown said the amount payable had not yet been finalised and remained subject to community engagement. GroundUp reported on 29 October 2026 that the Society's counsel said the Authority later paid the Society M8.2 million, and that on 20 October 2026 the High Court, before Acting Justice Tšebang Putsoane, made a settlement with the Authority an order of court: M89.9 million, payable within ninety days to 20 community associations, mostly in Thaba-Tseka, in individual amounts from M16.2 million down to M848,000, being the unpaid second tranche plus an 8 per cent increase since 2013. GroundUp's headline gives the figure as nearly M90 million. Those figures are GroundUp's reporting of the order, not the order itself. The same report says an Ombudsman report released in March 2026 put Phase 1 arrears at more than M142 million at the end of 2025.

extend.why: The Court of Appeal judgment of 7 November 2025 and the October 2026 M89.9 million settlement order enforce the Phase 1 In-Stream Flow Requirement policy. The World Bank's own Phase 1B completion report records that policy as developed, adopted and first paid out during its IBRD-43390 loan, treats compliance with it as a safeguards matter of the project it financed, and ties it to flows taken by the Bank-financed Katse and Mohale dams.
